In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the psychiatrist as administrator and leader is a role that is not yet fully defined.

the clinical skills and the administrative skills of the psychiatrist are similar but not identical, and that a psychiatrist can be a productive administrator only if his clinical training has been broad, his clinical practice has been varied, and his clinical experience has been deep and long.
the psychiatrist as administrator must be a clinician first.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we need to learn how to be both clinicians and administrators and that we need to be able to make the transition smoothly and without loss of identity.
the psychiatrist who moves from clinical work to administration should be prepared for a new role with new challenges.

the clinician who becomes an administrator must learn to apply his or her knowledge and skills to the organization as a whole, to the individuals who make up the organization, and to the relationship between the two.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the psychiatrist as an administrator and leader needs to understand the organizational context in which he or she is working.

the clinician who is moving from principle clinical responsibility into the role of principle administrative responsibility must be prepared to make the shift in behavior and to learn which administrative behaviors are facilitative and productive and which impede.
